4012a07987.d: Guruḥ sets into combustion (astamayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2025-Jun-10 21:12. At this moment guruḥ is at mr̥gaśīrṣam-4 mithunam (latitude 0°09′44.84″ S, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -1.90, elongation 10°10′02.26″ E of the Sun. Combustion (mAudhyam) is generally considered to weaken a graha's ability to give full results in its significations; undertakings connected with guruḥ are traditionally best avoided until it re-emerges.

4021cd13ef.d: Special vrata day for Ganesha. In this month, Ganesha is worshipped as bhālachandra-mahāgaṇapatiḥ. Fast during the day and pray to Ganesha after moonrise, chanting the shloka mentioned. When chaturthī tithi occurs on a Tuesday, it is known as aṅgārakī and is as sacred as a solar eclipse. Particularly special day for doing puja of Ganesha/Subrahmanya with naivedyam of modakam/millet flour respectively.
4021cd13ef.s:
𑌗𑌣𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌪𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍇𑌶 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌯𑌾।  
𑌕𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑍋𑌚𑌯𑍇𑌶𑌾𑌨 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌂 𑌚 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑍇॥  
  
𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌲𑍇𑌶𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌦𑍁𑌃𑌖𑍈𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍁𑌣𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍇 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍈 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌨𑍀𑌯𑍋 𑌗𑌣𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌪𑌃॥ (𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌮𑍍)  
𑌅𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑍋𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀 𑌭𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌨𑌾 𑌸𑌹।  
𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀 𑌭𑍂𑌮𑌿𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑍋𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌚𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌣𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌭𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 ௧௧௩.௬௦---  
𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀 𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍।  
𑌸𑌾𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌰𑌕𑌾 𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾॥

404e58656c.b: Observed on Paurṇamāsī tithi of Āśvayujaḥ (lunar) month (Niśīthaḥ/paraviddha).
404e58656c.d: Have to play Aksha kreeda only on this day and Ko-jagarti-Vratam (Lakshmi will ask “who are awake”). Vaalakhilya Rishi also mentioned Ko-jagarti Vratam.
404e58656c.s:
𑌨𑌿𑌶𑍀𑌥𑍇 𑌵𑌰𑌦𑌾 𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌮𑍀𑌃 𑌕𑍋 𑌜𑌾𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍀𑌤𑌿 𑌭𑌾𑌷𑌿𑌣𑍀।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍈 𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍈𑌃 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌡𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑌃॥

409360bd5a.d: Budhaḥ rises out of combustion (udayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2025-Sep-30 19:29. At this moment budhaḥ is at chitrā-1 kanyā (latitude 0°03′20.87″ S, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -0.56, elongation 12°51′16.75″ E of the Sun. Emergence from combustion restores a graha's full strength; this is generally considered an auspicious time to begin activities connected with budhaḥ's significations.

409591f4d3.d: Śukraḥ emerges from combustion into bAlya (infancy) on 2027-Sep-16 16:59. At this moment śukraḥ is at uttaraphalgunī-4 kanyā (latitude 1°15′23.57″ N, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -3.90, elongation 9°45′00.21″ E of the Sun. A graha in bAlya is likewise considered to give reduced results, for 5 days, before regaining its full strength.

40a7663bde.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′23.94″.
40a7663bde.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′23.94″, 0°37′06.38″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′43.28″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′36.88″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′07.22″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°37′54.32″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
40a7663bde.s:
𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌗𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍂𑌰𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇  
  
𑌷𑌣𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌭𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌭𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑍇 𑌯𑍌𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌭𑌮𑍍।  
--𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 (𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣)

40b0316f27.b: Observed on Kr̥ṣṇa-Aṣṭamī tithi of Phālgunaḥ (lunar) month (Aparāhṇaḥ/vyaapti).
40b0316f27.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌥𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃। 𑌤𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃 - 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚 𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃---  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌇𑌤𑌿। 𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 - 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃, 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 - 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌪𑍌𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌚 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌰𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍁 𑌚।   
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌬𑍋𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌉𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌃।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍂𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௧௯॥  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌚॥௨௦॥  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌥 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇।  
𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾॥௨௧॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌚 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌘𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌾𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌗𑌮𑍇।  
𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌯𑌾 𑌚𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌿 𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌿॥௨௨॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰 𑌉𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌃।  
𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌣𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍂𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍॥௨௩॥  
𑌤 𑌏𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑌸𑌃 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾 𑌨𑍃𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍈𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌮𑍋𑌘𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌷𑌃॥௨௪॥  
𑌏𑌷𑍁 𑌸𑍍‍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑍋 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌨𑍃𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௨௫॥

40b438cef2.d: Saptamī tithi on a Sunday is as sacred as a solar eclipse. Particularly good for worshipping Surya. When śukla saptamī is present at sunrise, it is called vijayā.
40b438cef2.s:
𑌅𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑍋𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀 𑌭𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌨𑌾 𑌸𑌹।  
𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀 𑌭𑍂𑌮𑌿𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑍋𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌚𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌣𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌭𑌾𑌃॥

40b96a3b83.d: Beginning of madhu-māsaḥ, marked by the transit of Sun into the 1st division of the tropical zodiac. Also marks the beginning of vasantar̥tuḥand the vernal equinox. While nirayana saṅkrānti's are widely observed, tropical saṅkrānti's are also equally sacred, and have similar puṇyakālas associated with them.
40b96a3b83.s:

40d8285d49.b: Observed on Śukla-Ṣaṣṭhī tithi of Caitraḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
40d8285d49.s:
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍇 𑌸𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌵  
𑌵𑍇𑌗𑌾𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍇 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍂𑌪𑍀।  
𑌊𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌵𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍌 𑌕𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌰𑍂𑌪𑍀 𑌸𑌦𑌾 𑌤𑍇  
𑌬𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍌 𑌬𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍌 𑌭𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌗𑍋𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌃॥  
---𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍇

40e0bd6a9e.b: Observed on Rēvatī nakshatra of Mithunam (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
40e0bd6a9e.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Eyarkon Kalikama Nayanmar, a devout Vellala from Tiruperumangalam in Ponni Nadu, was a dedicated follower of Bhagavan Shiva and belonged to the esteemed Eyarkudi family known for its military leaders. He was deeply troubled by the news that Sundaramurthi Nayanmar had utilised Bhagavan Shiva to resolve a personal dispute with his wife, which led him to question Sundaramurthi's devotion and his own piety.

In response to Kalikama Nayanmar's doubts, Bhagavan Shiva intervened by afflicting Kalikama Nayanmar with colic and informed him in a dream that only Sundaramurthi could cure it. However, Kalikama Nayanmar, staunch in his principles, chose to die rather than seek help from Sundaramurthi. Concurrently, Bhagavan Shiva instructed Sundaramurthi in a dream to heal Kalikama Nayanmar.

Upon Sundaramurthi's arrival, Kalikama Nayanmar had already ended his life. This act of defiance led to a dramatic scene where Sundaramurthi, in despair, attempted to take his own life. At this critical moment, Bhagavan Shiva's grace miraculously revived Kalikama Nayanmar, leading to a heartfelt reconciliation between the two devotees. Following this profound experience, Kalikama Nayanmar devoted his life to serving Bhagavan Shiva and His devotees, ultimately attaining a place in the divine abode.
40e0bd6a9e.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

4102d99f81.d: Pradosha Vratam. Fast during the day and perform śivapūjā in Pradosha Kala. Pradosha vratam is even more special, when if falls on a Friday, and is suitable for starting the vratam, for saubhāgyastrīsamr̥ddhyartham.
4102d99f81.s:
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑍇 𑌶𑌿𑌵𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌯𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌶𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌿॥  
𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑍋 𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰।  
𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍇𑌶 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌪𑌯𑌾 𑌹𑌰॥  
𑌮𑌦𑌨𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌨-𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌵𑌚𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿---  
𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾।  
𑌆𑌰𑌬𑍍𑌧𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌫𑌲𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌯𑍇॥  
𑌸𑍌𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌸𑌮𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾॥  
  
𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍂 𑌰𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌕𑍋𑌽𑌸𑌿  
𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍀 𑌆𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑍌  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌕𑌣𑍍𑌠𑍋𑌽𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍॥  
𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌹𑌲𑌂 𑌹𑌰 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌂  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸𑌪𑌦𑌿 𑌯𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌨𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍।  
𑌦𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌶𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌧𑌿 𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇  
𑌸 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑌶𑍁𑌪𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍁𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾 𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌾 𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌾 𑌶𑌿𑌵 𑌪𑌾𑌵𑌨𑍀𑌤𑌿  
𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌰 𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌿 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌕𑍂𑌟𑌃।  
𑌸𑌂𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑌾𑌯 𑌜𑌗𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌤𑍍  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌦𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾 𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍇𑌶𑌾𑌨 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌭𑌗𑍀𑌰𑌥𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌂 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌭𑍇𑌦𑌹𑍇𑌤𑌵𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌---  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍁𑌭𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌸𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌨𑍈𑌕𑌦𑍇𑌶𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑍇𑌽𑌧𑌿𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍂𑌨𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌪𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌦𑌿𑌨 𑌏𑌵  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌨𑍀𑌯𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍍।

This marks the third day of the festival, when Bhagavan Subrahmanya is in procession.

41d268774f.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌥𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃। 𑌤𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃 - 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚 𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃---  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌇𑌤𑌿। 𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 - 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃, 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 - 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌪𑍌𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌚 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌰𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍁 𑌚।   
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌬𑍋𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌉𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌇𑌤𑌿।

423f010ff5.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌥𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃। 𑌤𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃 - 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚 𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃---  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌇𑌤𑌿। 𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 - 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃, 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 - 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌪𑍌𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌚 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌰𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍁 𑌚।   
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌬𑍋𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌉𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌇𑌤𑌿।

4280b5dba9.b: Observed on Uttaraphalgunī nakshatra of Vr̥ścikaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
4280b5dba9.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe.

The 5th of them---Meypporul Nayanmar---a devout king of Sethi's hill tribes, was celebrated for his bravery, chivalry, and successful battles, creating a peaceful and prosperous kingdom. He deeply revered Bhagavan Shiva, seeing Him and His devotees as the embodiment of Absolute Truth, and held Shiva Bhaktas in high esteem, with daily prayers and festivals in temples.

His fame, however, stirred jealousy in Muthanathan, a neighbouring king. Muthanathan, defeated in battle, resorted to deceit, disguising himself as a Shiva Yogi to assassinate Nayanmar. Even as he lay dying from the betrayal, Nayanmar's concern was for the impostor's safety, instructing his guard to protect the assailant and honour him as a Shiva yogi as he appeared as one! His last words urged continued devotion and service to Shiva Bhaktas.

Bhagavan Shiva immediately manifested in front of him and bestowed his blessings with these words: Your unwavering devotion to my devotees, your boundless cosmic love, and your ability to see me even in a murderer have deeply impressed me. Due to these virtues, you are deserving of the Highest Abode, a place even the Devas aspire to but often cannot attain. You shall soon join me in My Divine Realm.'' After imparting this blessing, Bhagavan Shiva vanished, and the Nayanmar, aptly named as 'one who regards God as the sole reality' (meypporuḷ), ascended to Shiva's divine abode.
4280b5dba9.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

42f6a280b1.b: Partial solar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈5.9 of 12 aṅgulas), Sun at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
42f6a280b1.d: Magnitude: 49% of the solar diameter is covered (parimāṇa ≈5.9 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 03:17►17:43 (from 4 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra punarvasuḥ/puṣyaḥ/āśrēṣā (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or anūrādhā (anujanma) or uttaraprōṣṭhapadā (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: karkaṭaḥ, siṁhaḥ, dhanuḥ, mēṣaḥ get more ashubha phala, vr̥śchikaḥ, makaraḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam somewhat ashubha, kanyā, tulā, kumbhaḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

434cebf18c.d: Jyaiṣhṭha-māsaḥ begins today --- In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should fashion an image of Kañjaja (i.e., Brahmā, born from a lotus) using flour (piṣṭa) and install it along with a pedestal (vedikā). Worship it with flowers, perfumes, various garments, and ornaments. By doing so, one is honored in the realm of Brahmā or Sūrya (pāṭhāntaram) for more than a hundred crore years! In Vamana Purana, it is said that, to please Trivikrama, one should perform dāna of a pot of water, a cow, a fan made from palmyra leaves (tālavṛnta), and sandalwood.

439d32aa51.d: Every year, on Pongal day, there is a unique festival celebrated in the Madurai Meenakshi temple, to commemorate a unique happening, when Abhisheka Pandian ruled over Madurai. Once, the King was desirous of knowing the greatness of a saint in the temple, and requested him to demonstrate his powers by feeding a sugarcane to a stone elephant (sculpture). This festival celebrates this event, where the King was bewildered by the powers of the saint, who eventually blessed the King and soldiers.

43dd4beefc.d: This Sarvajñātman, who was born to Vardhana got initiated into asceticism even before the age of seven by Śrī Śaṅkara himself on being delighted to have had debate with him on the banks of river Tāmraparṇi; he spent seventy years along with Sureśvara in that Pīṭha and then lived in that Maṭha for forty-two years. The sage known as Sarvajña attained union with his own Self by doing service at the lotus feet of Śrī Padmapāda, who was dear to the Ācārya (Śrī Śaṅkara) and imparting the unparallel doctrine through Cinmudrā to the saint by name Brahmasvarūpa who served with love and faith at the feet of the master who was holding the pontiff-dom of the Dvāravatī maṭha. The sage Sarvajñātman whose works such as Saṁkṣepaśārīraka showed clearly/elaborately the collective meaning of the words hidden in the great commentatorial works on Advaita merged in the Supreme on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha in the Nala year of the Kali era 2737 at Kāñci Śrī Śaṅkara Maṭha.
43dd4beefc.s:

𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍀𑌠𑍇 𑌸𑌸𑍁𑌰𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌨𑌯𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌯𑌃 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌤𑌿𑌂

𑌆𑌚𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌚𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌭𑍋𑌜𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍀𑌸𑍇𑌵𑌨𑌾𑌦𑍍  
𑌊𑌢𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌵𑌤𑍀𑌮𑌠𑌾𑌯 𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌯𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍇।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌪𑌦𑌾𑌯 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌤𑍁𑌲𑌂 𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑌨𑍍-  
𑌨𑍇𑌵𑍈𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌗𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌜𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌹𑌸𑌾 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍋 𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌿𑌃॥௮॥  
𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌦𑍈𑌃 𑌸 𑌹𑌯𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌨𑌯𑌨𑍈𑌰𑍍 (௨௭௩௭) 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑌲𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑍇  
𑌲𑌿𑌲𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌮𑌨𑍁 𑌮𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌯𑌶𑍈𑌲𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇।  
𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌕𑌲𑌿𑌤𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑌦𑌂 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌪𑌶𑌾𑌰𑍀𑌰𑌕-  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌖𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌸𑍂𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌗𑌹𑌨𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌃 𑌪𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍋𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌯𑌃॥௯॥  
—𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌮𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌰𑍀

440393acc9.b: Observed on Śatabhiṣak nakshatra of Kanyā (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
440393acc9.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

This Nayanmar, a minor chieftain from Tiru Munaipadi, was a fervent devotee of Bhagavan Shiva and a staunch supporter of Shaivism. On every Tiruvathirai day, he would hold special Pujas, feed Shiva devotees regardless of their appearance, and generously offer each devotee a hundred gold coins.

During one such event, a devotee arrived with his body covered solely in sacred ashes, completely naked, causing discomfort among the other devotees. The Nayanmar, perceiving this, fell at the devotee's feet, and demonstrated his profound respect by not only feeding the naked devotee with greater reverence but also by offering him double the usual gift — 200 gold coins! This incident highlights the Nayanmar's deep understanding and acceptance that every devotee is an embodiment of Bhagavan Shiva, regardless of their external appearance.
440393acc9.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

4463f73a24.d: This Saccidānandaghana with a firm control over senses, conversant with various languages—was a Telugu brahmin named Timmaṇṇa, son of Prauḍha Rāmaṇṇa became the Jagadguru from region on the banks of river Chandrabhāga. Renovating the huge dilapidated maṭha, He remained happily in Kāñci itself by devoting himself every day in the worship of Devī Kāmākṣī. He, the benevolent great preceptor Saccidānandaghana having travelled upto Himalayas attained liberation on the sixth day of dark fortnight of the month Bhādrapada (Mahālaya Pakṣa) in the year Khara. He was also known as Bhāṣaparameṣṭi and his preceptorship was for twenty years.

𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌷𑌾𑌭𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌪𑍀 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌮𑌕𑍁𑌲𑌧𑌨𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌢𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍍𑌣𑌸𑍂𑌨𑍁𑌃  
𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌲𑌿𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌨𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌰𑌭𑍂𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍀𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌕𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌪𑍀𑌠𑌂 𑌮𑌠𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍁𑌲𑌂 𑌜𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯 𑌨𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌂  
𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌕𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌃 𑌸𑍁𑌖𑌮𑍍 𑌅𑌵𑌸𑌦𑌸𑍌 𑌸𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌸𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌃॥௬௪॥  
𑌖𑌰𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌷𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍍 𑌅𑌖𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌧𑌿𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸 𑌸𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌘𑌨𑍋 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌲𑌯𑌮𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌃॥௬௫॥  
—𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌮𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌰𑍀

448066a2bd.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌥𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃। 𑌤𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃 - 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚 𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃---  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌇𑌤𑌿। 𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 - 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃, 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 - 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌪𑍌𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌚 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌰𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍁 𑌚।   
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌬𑍋𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌉𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌇𑌤𑌿।

4493c71b13.b: Partial lunar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈3.0 of 12 aṅgulas), Moon at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
4493c71b13.d: The eclipse is already in progress at moonrise (grastodaya). Umbral magnitude: 0.25 (parimāṇa ≈3.0 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 09:34►19:53 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra maghā/pūrvaphalgunī/uttaraphalgunī (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or pūrvāṣāḍhā (anujanma) or apabharaṇī (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: siṁhaḥ, kanyā, makaraḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ get more ashubha phala, dhanuḥ, kumbhaḥ, mēṣaḥ, karkaṭaḥ somewhat ashubha, tulā, vr̥śchikaḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.
4493c71b13.r: - Food-restriction timing and graha-shanti nakshatra/rashi lists follow this pancAnga's "General notes for all grahanas" instructions.

456e92220b.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Enadinatha Nayanmar, a toddy tapper (Shanar) by profession and a fervent devotee of Bhagavan Shiva, hailed from Eyinanur in the Chola Kingdom, located near Kumbakonam. The 9th of the Nayanmars, he revered not only Bhagavan Shiva but also any person who bore the mark of Vibhuti, the sacred ash, symbolizing the destruction of ego, illusions, and desires, leading to spiritual liberation.

Enadinatha Nayanmar, also an expert swordsman, earned his livelihood by training princes in fencing. He dedicated his earnings to serving Shiva Bhaktas, earning him popularity but also the envy of Atisuran, a less competent and vice-ridden rival in the same profession. Atisuran, desiring to defeat Enadinatha, challenged him to a fight, resulting in a fierce battle where many lives were lost, and Atisuran fled.

The next day, Atisuran proposed a one-on-one duel at a secluded location. Enadinatha agreed and met Atisuran at the agreed place. However, when Atisuran revealed the sacred ash on his forehead, Enadinatha, in his devotion to Bhagavan Shiva, refused to fight, recognizing Atisuran as a Shiva Bhakta. Despite his unwillingness to harm Atisuran, Enadinatha kept his sword, not wanting to compel Atisuran to sin by killing an unarmed person. Atisuran then took the opportunity to kill Enadinatha.

Bhagavan Shiva, impressed by Enadinatha's profound devotion and self-sacrifice for the sake of the sacred ash, appeared before him as he fell, and took him to His divine abode. This story highlights the immense reverence and selflessness of Enadinatha Nayanmar in his devotion to Bhagavan Shiva and His devotees.
456e92220b.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

4577e971f1.b: Observed on Śukla-Dvitīyā tithi of Bhādrapadaḥ (lunar) month (Prātaḥ/puurvaviddha).
4577e971f1.s:
𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌜𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌨𑌃।  
𑌮𑍍𑌲𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌕𑌿𑌰𑍂𑌪𑍋 𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿॥  
𑌅𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌉𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌯𑌤𑍍 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌮𑍍  
𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌯𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌵𑌲𑍍𑌲𑍀---  
𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌕𑌿𑌜𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍀। 𑌸𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿𑌨𑍀 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌾।   
𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌭𑍇 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌰𑍇।  
𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌲𑌗𑍍𑌨𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌃 𑌕𑌲𑌿𑌕𑌿𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌧𑍃𑌤𑍍॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।

45bb1b4b3a.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥  
𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌦𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌆𑌸𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---   
𑌯𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌤𑌦𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌲𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌲𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌹𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌃---  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁।  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥

4629839ec7.d: Gaṅgādharagīṣpatiḥ, known as Subhadra, son of Kāñci Bhadragiri, got initiated in the twelfth year of age by Śrī Vidyāghana whom He had served became a realised soul when He as twenty-four years old and reached the eternal abode of Śrīvidyā and Śrī Śiva. He, the Omnipotent, omniscient and pure reached the eternal abode by his glory on the first day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra of the year Sarvadhari.
4629839ec7.s:
𑌸𑍂𑌨𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌗𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌃 𑌸𑍁𑌭𑌦𑍍𑌰 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑌃 𑌕𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌚𑍍𑌯(𑌕𑌪𑍍𑌯?)𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍇  
𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌸𑌂𑌯𑌮𑌮𑍍 𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌨𑍁𑌚𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌆𑌚𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌘𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌧𑌰𑌗𑍀𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌸 𑌚 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌂𑌶𑍇 𑌵𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌶𑌿𑌵𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌧𑍃𑌤𑍇𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌦𑌂 𑌶𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌤𑌮𑍍॥௩௦॥  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌧𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌣𑌿 𑌸 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌧𑌾𑌰𑌕𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌰𑌧𑌿𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑍍 𑌅𑌰𑍍𑌜𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌅𑌰𑍍𑌜𑍁𑌨𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌶𑌸𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌦𑌿𑌮𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇𑌽𑌨𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌮 𑌮𑌹𑌸𑌾 𑌜𑌗𑌾𑌮 𑌹॥௩௧॥  
—𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌮𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌰𑍀

4680f6e5ca.d: Offer Akasha Dipam for this entire month, in the evening, on a high place (pillar?). Light lamps using gingelly oil with eight wicks.
4680f6e5ca.s:
𑌤𑍁𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂  𑌤𑌿𑌲𑌤𑍈𑌲𑍇𑌨  𑌸𑌾𑌯𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍇  𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍇।  
𑌆𑌕𑌾𑌶𑌦𑍀𑌪𑌂  𑌯𑍋  𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌂  𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌂  𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿।  
𑌮𑌹𑌤𑍀𑌂  𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿  𑌰𑍂𑌪-𑌸𑍌𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌯-𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌦𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌦𑌾𑌮𑍋𑌦𑌰𑌾𑌯  𑌨𑌭𑌸𑌿  𑌤𑍁𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂  𑌲𑍋𑌲𑌯𑌾  𑌸𑌹।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌪𑌂  𑌤𑍇  𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌮𑌿  𑌨𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌯  𑌵𑍇𑌧𑌸𑍇॥

46ddb930ea.b: Observed on Śukla-Ēkādaśī tithi of Āṣāḍhaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
46ddb930ea.d:
The special Chaaturmasya vratam begins on Ekadashi, coinciding with Shayana Ekadashi. In each of the months, specific vratams are observed, with restrictions on various foods. On each of the next four shuddha dvadashis, beginning with tomorrow, a vratam starts. In āṣāḍha-śravaṇa, śākavratam is observed; in śravaṇa--bhādrapada, dadhi-vratam is observed; in bhādrapada-āśvina, payō-vratam is observed, and in āśvina--kārtika, dvidala-vratam is observed.
Pradakshina to Pippala; Deeparadhana in temple; Saraswati Pooja.
46ddb930ea.s:
𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌨𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂---  
𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌹𑍇 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌘𑌣𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌦𑍀𑌨𑍍 𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌯𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌬𑌹𑍂𑌨𑍍।  
𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌯 𑌮𑌹𑌤𑍀𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌮𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌚𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍।  
𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌨𑌾𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌥𑌾---  
𑌸𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌿 𑌜𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌥𑍇𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌦𑌾𑌹𑍃𑌤𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑌗𑌵𑌦𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌸𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌿 𑌜𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌥𑍇 𑌜𑌗𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌮𑍍।  
𑌵𑌿𑌬𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌿 𑌬𑍁𑌧𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵 𑌸𑌚𑌰𑌾𑌚𑌰𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌪𑍇 𑌭𑍋𑌗𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌥𑍇 𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌥𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌿।  
𑌚𑌾𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌨𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌿 𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌮𑍀𑌪𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌮।  
𑌲𑌬𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌨𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌖𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌷𑌿𑌤𑌭𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍃𑌕𑌾।  
𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍋 𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌪𑌨𑌾𑌵𑌧𑌿।  
𑌇𑌮𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑌂 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍁 𑌮𑍇𑌽𑌚𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤॥  
𑌇𑌦𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌮𑌯𑌾 𑌦𑍇𑌵 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍀𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌵।  
𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍀𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍇𑌵 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌮𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑍇 𑌜𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌨।  
𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌥 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍇𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌨𑌿𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌣𑍇 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌕𑌂 𑌦𑌧𑌿 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾।  
𑌦𑍁𑌗𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇 𑌚𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌷𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌚𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌂 𑌚𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌬𑍁 𑌜𑌮𑍍𑌬𑍀𑌰𑌂 𑌬𑍀𑌜𑌪𑍂𑌰𑌕𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌅𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌶𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍋𑌰𑌨𑌿𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌦𑌗𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌮𑌸𑍂𑌰𑌂 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌂𑌸𑌂 𑌚𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌧𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌮𑌿𑌷𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌰𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌶𑌲𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌫𑌲𑌮𑍂𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌮𑌾𑌷𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌸𑍂𑌰𑌂 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌚॥  
𑌵𑍃𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌕𑌂 𑌚 𑌕𑌲𑌿𑌙𑍍𑌗 𑌚 𑌸𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌿 𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌹𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌶𑍀 𑌨 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌭𑌾𑌕𑍍॥  
𑌹𑍈𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌗𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑌪𑌾𑌲𑌕𑌙𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍀𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌂 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌕𑌂 𑌹𑌿𑌮𑌲𑍋𑌚𑌿𑌕𑌾॥  
𑌪𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌿𑌕𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌶𑌾𑌕𑌂 𑌚 𑌮𑍂𑌲𑌕𑌂 𑌕𑍇𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍇𑌤𑌰𑌤𑍍।  
𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌂 𑌸𑍈𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌵𑌸𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌗𑌵𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑌧𑌿𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌪𑌿𑌷𑍀॥  
𑌪𑌯𑍋𑌨𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌸𑌾𑌰𑌂 𑌚 𑌪𑌨𑌸𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌰𑍀𑌤𑌕𑍀𑌃।  
𑌪𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌪𑌲𑍀 𑌜𑍀𑌰𑌕𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌨𑌾𑌗𑌰𑌂 𑌚𑌾𑌥 𑌤𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌣𑍀॥  
𑌕𑌦𑌲𑍀𑌲𑌵𑌲𑍀𑌧𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌫𑌲𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌗𑍁𑌡𑌮𑍈𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌵𑌮𑍍।  
𑌅𑌤𑍈𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌯𑍋 𑌹𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌣𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌚𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍇॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
[𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌲𑌵𑌣𑌶𑌾𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍। 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌗𑍌𑌡𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍋 𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌃।  
𑌸 𑌚 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌨 𑌏𑌵 𑌹𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍍। 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌲𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌥𑌃।  
𑌕𑌙𑍍𑌗𑍁 𑌕𑌾𑌙𑍍𑌗 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌭𑌾𑌷𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌮𑍍। 𑌹𑌿𑌲𑌮𑍋𑌚𑌿𑌕𑌾 𑌗𑍌𑌡𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌹𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌸𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌃 𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌾𑌕𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌶𑌾𑌕𑌃 𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌤𑌦𑍇𑌶𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌃 𑌶𑌾𑌕𑌃। 𑌕𑍇𑌮𑍁𑌕𑌂 𑌕𑍇𑌮𑍍𑌬𑍁 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌗𑍌𑌡𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌮𑍍।  
𑌮𑍂𑌲𑌕𑌮𑍍। 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌃 𑌸𑍂𑌰𑌣𑌃। 𑌨𑌾𑌗𑌰𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌠𑌿𑌃।  
𑌲𑌵𑌲𑍀 𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌆𑌂𑌵𑌳𑍀 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾। 𑌹𑌰𑌫𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌵𑌡𑍀 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌦𑍇𑌶𑍇 𑌅𑌤𑍈𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌕𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌉𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌣𑌮𑍍।]  
𑌨𑍃𑌸𑌿𑌂𑌹𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌚𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇---  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌣𑍇 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌕𑌂 𑌦𑌧𑌿 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾।  
𑌦𑍁𑌗𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌦𑌲𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜𑍇𑌤𑍍। 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑍇---  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌦𑌲𑌂 𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌬𑍀𑌜𑌕𑌮𑍍। 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌦𑌲𑌂 𑌚 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵---  
𑌮𑌾𑌷𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌗𑌮𑌸𑍂𑌰𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌚𑌣𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌕𑍁𑌲𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌥𑌕𑌾𑌃।  
𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌵𑌾 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌮𑌾𑌷𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌆𑌢𑌕𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌦𑌲𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌨𑍂𑌤𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌿 𑌜𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍। 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌚---  
𑌬𑍀𑌜𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌭𑍂𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌦𑌲𑌂 𑌚𑌾𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌰𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌾।  
𑌦𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌦𑌲𑌂 𑌤𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌗𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇। 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌏𑌤𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌨𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍇---  
𑌚𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌨𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍍। 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵---  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌦𑌲𑌂 𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌬𑍀𑌜𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑍃𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌕𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌜𑌮𑍍𑌬𑍀𑌰𑌂 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌮𑌾𑌷𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑍂𑌲𑌕𑌂 𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍂𑌲𑌕𑌮𑍍।  
𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌂 𑌚𑍇𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍁𑌦𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌂 𑌚 𑌚𑌾𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌬𑍁𑌧𑌃।  
𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌬𑍀𑌜𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌣𑍇𑌨 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍇𑌧𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑍃𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌚𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑍋𑌷𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌮𑍍। 𑌏𑌵𑌂 𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍂𑌲𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿।

46e7957ce3.d: The Soma-Chitra combination is also special for observing nakta-vratams as per Agni Purana.
46e7957ce3.s:
𑌅𑌗𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌹𑌿।  
...  
𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌭𑌸𑍋𑌮𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌿 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍁𑌖𑍀 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௧௯௫-௩॥

46f761a279.d: Budhaḥ rises out of combustion (udayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2025-Aug-08 11:27. At this moment budhaḥ is at puṣyaḥ-3 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 3°54′24.56″ S, moving vakra (retrograde)), magnitude +2.72, elongation 11°51′18.49″ W of the Sun. Emergence from combustion restores a graha's full strength; this is generally considered an auspicious time to begin activities connected with budhaḥ's significations.

471b2c8271.d: Special vrata day for Ganesha. In this month, Ganesha is worshipped as ēkadanta-mahāgaṇapatiḥ. Fast during the day and pray to Ganesha after moonrise, chanting the shloka mentioned.
471b2c8271.s:
𑌗𑌣𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌪𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍇𑌶 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌯𑌾।  
𑌕𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑍋𑌚𑌯𑍇𑌶𑌾𑌨 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌂 𑌚 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑍇॥  
  
𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌲𑍇𑌶𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌦𑍁𑌃𑌖𑍈𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍁𑌣𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍇 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍈 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌨𑍀𑌯𑍋 𑌗𑌣𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌪𑌃॥ (𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌮𑍍)

472dec0488.b: Observed on Śukla-Dvādaśī tithi of Bhādrapadaḥ (lunar) month (Madhyāhnaḥ/puurvaviddha).
472dec0488.d: Vamana Jayanti---Avatara Dinam of Shri Mahavishnu, born as Vamana Murti to Aditi and Kashyapa Maharshi.
472dec0488.s:
𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌭𑍁𑌃।  
𑌅𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌜𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌂 𑌬𑌲𑌿𑌮𑍋𑌜𑌸𑌾॥  
𑌅𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌉𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌯𑌤𑍍 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌮𑍍  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑍋𑌵𑌾𑌚  
𑌜𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌯 𑌭𑌗𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮 𑌨𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍇।  
𑌨𑌮𑍋 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌾𑌯 𑌨𑌮𑍋 𑌨𑌮𑌃॥௨௫॥  
𑌨𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌯 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌯 𑌵𑍇𑌧𑌸𑍇।  
𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌯 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌪𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾𑌯 𑌶𑌿𑌪𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌯 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑍇॥௨௬॥  
𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍍  
𑌅𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌂 𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌹𑍁𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍋 𑌭𑌵𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌪𑌤𑍀𑌶 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌂  
𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌤𑍋 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌗𑌭𑍀𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௨௭॥  
𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑍈 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌜𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌰𑌜𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌜𑌾𑌪𑌤𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌸𑌿 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃  
𑌦𑌿𑌵𑍌𑌕𑌸𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂  
𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌣𑌂 𑌨𑍌𑌰𑌿𑌵 𑌮𑌜𑍍𑌜𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌸𑍁॥௨௮॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌮𑌹𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍇 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌶𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌦𑌿𑌶𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍇𑌦𑍁𑌃 𑌸𑌲𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌶𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌾  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌜𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾 𑌋𑌤𑌵𑍋 𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍌𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑌿𑌰𑌗𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌜𑌿𑌹𑍍𑌵𑌾  
𑌗𑌾𑌵𑍋 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌹𑍃𑌷𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌨𑌗𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚॥௪॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌣𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌭𑌿𑌜𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍁𑌃।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇 𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌕𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌜𑍍𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮 𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌣𑌮𑍍॥௫॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌗𑌤𑍋 𑌨𑍃𑌪।  
𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌸𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌰𑍇𑌃॥௬॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌮𑌹𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍇 𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃॥

4906067265.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Satti Nayanmar, born into a Vellala family, hailed from Varinjiyur in the Chola kingdom. He was deeply devoted to Bhagavan Shiva and held great respect for Bhagavan's devotees. Satti Nayanmar was so committed to honoring these devotees that he could not bear to hear any slander against them. In his zeal to protect their dignity, he would go to the extreme measure of cutting out the tongue of anyone who spoke ill of Bhagavan Shiva's devotees. Recognizing the purity and intensity of Satti Nayanmar's devotion, Bhagavan Shiva bestowed his divine grace upon him.
4906067265.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

𑌕𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑍋𑌚𑌯𑍇𑌶𑌾𑌨 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌂 𑌚 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑍇॥  
  
𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌲𑍇𑌶𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌦𑍁𑌃𑌖𑍈𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍁𑌣𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍇 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍈 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌨𑍀𑌯𑍋 𑌗𑌣𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌪𑌃॥ (𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌮𑍍)

4969703e8f.b: Observed on Śukla-Saptamī tithi of Māghaḥ (lunar) month (Prāktanāruṇōdayaḥ/paraviddha).
4969703e8f.s:
𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍌 𑌰𑌥𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍋 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌕𑌰𑌃।  
𑌸𑌾 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌃 𑌕𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌯𑌾 𑌰𑌥𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀॥௧௨௯॥  
  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌹𑍁𑌤𑌂 𑌚𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌦𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌶𑌮𑌨𑌂 𑌭𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌤𑌯𑍇 𑌮𑌤𑌮𑍍॥௧௩௦॥  
---𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌕𑍌𑌮𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍇  
  
𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌣𑌤𑍁𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌹𑌿 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌾 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀।  
𑌅𑌰𑍁𑌣𑍋𑌦𑌯𑌵𑍇𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌫𑌲𑌮𑍍॥௬௩॥  
---𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌸𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌿𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍇𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍇  
  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍇---  
𑌨𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌰𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌾𑌯 𑌰𑌸𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑌤𑌯𑍇 𑌨𑌮𑌃।  
𑌅𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌕 𑌨𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌵 𑌨𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌪𑍇 𑌵𑌸𑍁𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍇।  
𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌾𑌰𑌭𑍇॥  
𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍇 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌿 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌪𑌿𑌕𑍇।  
𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌹𑌰 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌿 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌮𑌯𑌾 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌸𑍁 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍁।  
𑌤𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌰𑍋𑌗𑌂 𑌚 𑌶𑍋𑌕𑌂 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌕𑌰𑍀 𑌹𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀॥  
𑌏𑌤𑌜𑍍𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌮𑌨𑍋𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍-𑌕𑌾𑌯𑌜𑌂 𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌤𑌾𑌽𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌚 𑌯𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌃॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇।

49cbaf6eb5.b: Observed on Aśvinī nakshatra of Makaraḥ (sidereal solar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
49cbaf6eb5.d:
In the ancient town of Tirunelveli, a devout worshipper of Bhagavan Shiva named Vedabhattar performed daily rituals for Bhagavan Shiva and provided food to the needy. Over time, his wealth diminished, but Vedabhattar continued his offerings and worship by seeking support from the local community. One day, he left paddy (rice grains) drying under the sun to prepare an offering for the temple, and went to bathe in the Tamraparni River. Suddenly, dark clouds gathered, and it began to rain heavily, threatening to ruin the drying paddy. Vedabhattar, anxious about his offering, prayed to Bhagavan Shiva and rushed back, only to find that a divine miracle had occurred: the paddy was untouched by rain, shielded as if by an invisible fence.

This miracle led to the town being named Tirunelveli, meaning “the place where the paddy was fenced.” This event is commemorated annually at the Nellaiappar Temple in Tirunelveli with special rituals and reenactments. (See https://www.vikatan.com/spiritual/thiruvilaiyadal-related-event-recreated-in-nellaiappar-temple-in-nellai)

4a205c4ab0.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śukraḥ in śravaṇaḥ makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°41′09.65″.
4a205c4ab0.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°41′09.65″, 0°41′02.28″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at śravaṇaḥ-4 makaraḥ (latitude 2°00′24.72″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.28, elongation 5°47′39.18″ E). śukraḥ at śravaṇaḥ-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°19′15.08″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 5°35′40.02″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4a46db2395.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śukraḥ in āśrēṣā karkaṭaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°30′35.96″.
4a46db2395.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°30′35.96″, 0°30′28.64″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at āśrēṣā-3 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°44′30.53″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -2.04, elongation 1°45′13.95″ W). śukraḥ at āśrēṣā-3 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°13′54.57″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 1°14′55.78″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4a8d47c510.d: Budhaḥ sets into combustion (astamayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2028-Mar-22 03:45. At this moment budhaḥ is at śatabhiṣak-4 kumbhaḥ (latitude 2°17′51.35″ S, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -0.39, elongation 18°38′46.66″ W of the Sun. Combustion (mAudhyam) is generally considered to weaken a graha's ability to give full results in its significations; undertakings connected with budhaḥ are traditionally best avoided until it re-emerges.

4af44efa5f.b: Observed on Śukla-Prathamā tithi of Caitraḥ (lunar) month (Aparāhṇaḥ/vyaapti). The event occurred in 4518 (Kali era).
4af44efa5f.d: He, as per the suggestions of the Sāyaṇa Mādhava, having commissioned the eight saints disciples to protect the tenets of Advaita and to check the development of the faith of Madhva in Karnataka, despite the unbearable separation from the master preceptor Vidyātīrtha, returned from Himalayas and under his (master’s) directions held the responsibilities of the Kāmakoṭi Maṭha. Son of Balachandra Makhi of Madhyārjuna, by name Maheśa (before initiation), having received initiation into asceticism from Vidyātīrtha, popularising among people Advaita among the systems and dispelling the ignorance caused by dvaita, the head of nine Maṭhas, the Navaśaṅkara, headed the Kāmakoṭi Pīṭha for thirty-two years. He the pleasing one, the great preceptor with a sweet speech, the intelligent One, adored by all in the world, shed his physical body on the pratipad of bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha of the year Durmukhi; entered at once into his effulgence. This preceptor Śrī Abhinva Śaṅkara or Śaṅkarānanda also known as Navamaṭhīnātha, was the founder of nine Maṭhas—Śṛṅgeri etc. adept in destroying the schools of Madhva, the one who made the idol Varadarāja appear as Bhagavan Śiva to wipe off the predominance of Vaiṣṇavism, adored by the king Bukka, renowned everywhere attained siddhi near Kāṅcipuram. This preceptor is the one who initiated the tradition of Śrīvidya mudrā.

4bb1512585.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°54′42.78″.
4bb1512585.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°54′42.78″, 0°54′30.01″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°07′32.66″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.97, elongation 14°48′02.43″ E). śukraḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°12′49.88″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 14°41′58.87″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4c4117042b.b: Observed on Puṣyaḥ nakshatra of Vr̥ṣabhaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
4c4117042b.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Nami Nandi Adigal, a devout Brahmana from Emaperur in the Chola kingdom, dedicated his life to worshipping Bhagavan Shiva in Tiruvarur. One day, driven by a desire to light numerous lamps in the temple as extolled in the Shiva Agamas, he sought ghee from a nearby house. However, the Jaina inhabitant mockingly suggested using water instead. Distressed, Nandi Adigal prayed to Bhagavan Shiva and was divinely instructed to use water from a nearby tank for lighting the lamps. Miraculously, the lamps burned brightly with water, astonishing the Jainas and leading to a decline in Jainism as people turned to Shaivism.

Recognising his devotion, the Chola king appointed Nandi Adigal as the head of the temple. He zealously conducted the Panguni Uttaram festival at Tirumanali, drawing worshippers of all varṇas. One night, feeling unpurified by the contact with people of various varṇas, he hesitated to enter his home. As he waited for his wife to bring him water to bathe, he fell asleep and dreamt of Bhagavan Shiva, who revealed that all born in Tiruvarur were His ganas! Awakening, Nandi Adigal narrated this story to his wife, and performed his worship. In the morning, he went back to Tiruvarur and saw that the people of Tiruvarur bore the form of Bhagavan Shiva! As he prostrated to them, they all resumed their original forms --- thus a divine Lila being enacted by Bhagavan.

Settling in Tiruvarur, Nandi Adigal devoted himself to serving Bhagavan and His devotees, earning praise as 'Anipon' (pure gold) from the Nayanmar Appar. He ultimately attained the sublime abode of Bhagavan Shiva, exemplifying pure devotion and service.

4cc5ee5b45.d: He, Soma, initiated with the title Bodhendra by the preceptor Paraśivendra adorned the Pīṭha and visiting countries in the palanquin exquisitely decked with gems offered by Bhoja, the king of Dhārā, inculcating faith in the principles of Advaita in the minds of those who venerated him on the path safeguarded the Maṭha from the invaders (mlechas) with the help of the minister of the Kashmiri King Kalaśa.  Having stayed in the Pīṭha for thirty-seven years, He reached the Supreme Abode at Aruṇācala on the New moon day of the month Āṣāḍha in the year Īśvara. This preceptor Bodhendra, also known as Sānandrānanda, was honoured for poetical excellence by Kings—Bhoja, Kalaśeśvara and others and was intent on travelling through the earth.

4ce02cbc71.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′22.99″.
4ce02cbc71.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′22.99″, 0°37′05.43″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′43.03″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′37.13″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′06.02″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°37′54.50″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4e24eeb0cf.b: Observed on Śukla-Tr̥tīyā tithi of Caitraḥ (lunar) month (Madhyāhnaḥ/puurvaviddha).

4e3c2b058c.b: Observed on Amāvāsyā tithi of Siṁhaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/paraviddha).
4e3c2b058c.d: One must collect darbha on this day. Darbha collected on this day remains fit for use throughout, without any dosha of yātayāmam.
4e3c2b058c.s:
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌾𑌰𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌯𑌃---  
𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌶𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌟𑌨𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌮𑌰𑍀𑌚𑌿𑌃-  
𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍇 𑌨𑌭𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌯𑍋 𑌮𑌤𑌃।  
𑌅𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌿𑌯𑍋𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌃॥  
𑌕𑍁𑌶𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌟𑌨𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁---  
𑌕𑍁𑌶𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌵𑌸𑌤𑍇 𑌰𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌶𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌕𑍇𑌶𑌵𑌃।  
𑌕𑍁𑌶𑌮𑍂𑌲𑍇 𑌵𑌸𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌾 𑌕𑍁𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌿॥  
𑌅𑌥 𑌕𑍁𑌶𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌟𑌨𑍇𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌲𑌿𑌖𑌿𑌤𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌃---  
𑍐 𑌵𑌿𑌰𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌨𑌾 𑌸𑌹𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌨 𑌪𑌰𑌮𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌿𑌨𑌿𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌜।  
𑌨𑍁𑌦 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌣𑌿 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌭 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌰𑍋 𑌭𑌵॥

4e6062e427.d: Śukraḥ rises out of combustion (udayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2027-Sep-16 16:59. At this moment śukraḥ is at uttaraphalgunī-4 kanyā (latitude 1°15′23.57″ N, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -3.90, elongation 9°45′00.21″ E of the Sun. Emergence from combustion restores a graha's full strength; this is generally considered an auspicious time to begin activities connected with śukraḥ's significations.

4e794466de.b: Observed on Śukla-Tr̥tīyā tithi of Vaiśākhaḥ (lunar) month (Sāṅgavaḥ/paraviddha).
4e794466de.d: Daanam of Dadhyodanam, Vyanjanam, Chatram, Paduka, Udaka Kumbham, Mangos, Jackfruit; Lakshmi Narayana Pooja; Gauri Pooja;
4e794466de.s:
𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌪𑍂𑌜𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌸𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌂 𑌜𑌗𑌦𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌮𑍍।  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌧𑍂𑌪𑌵𑌿𑌲𑍇𑌪𑌨𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌃---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌤𑍋𑌯𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌿𑌲𑍍𑌬𑌿𑌷𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌹𑍋𑌮𑍋 𑌯𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌶𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍।  
𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌮𑌦𑌨𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌨𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇---  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣 𑌉𑌵𑌾𑌚  
𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌨𑌾𑌽𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌿𑌂 𑌬𑌹𑍍𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌾।  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍃𑌣𑍁॥௧॥  
𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌪𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌚 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌹𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍍॥௨॥  
𑌆𑌦𑌿𑌃 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌮𑌨𑍀 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍌𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌯𑌿𑌨𑍀॥௩॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾 𑌮𑌹𑍋𑌦𑌯𑍇 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥 𑌵𑌣𑌿𑌗𑌾𑌸𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌸 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌃।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌂𑌵𑌦𑌃 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌵𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌕𑌃॥௪॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍈𑌕𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌟𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌬𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌕𑍁𑌲𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌨𑍍।  
𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑌾 𑌵𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌾 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌰𑍋𑌹𑌿𑌣𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾॥௫॥  
𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌬𑍁𑌧𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌸𑌾 𑌸𑍁𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌫𑌲𑌾।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑍀𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍇𑌵 𑌹𑌿॥௬॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌗𑍃𑌹𑌮𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌦𑌕𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௭॥  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌬𑍃𑌹𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌲𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌮𑌲𑍇𑌨 𑌚।  
𑌯𑌵𑌗𑍋𑌧𑍂𑌮𑌚𑌣𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍂𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌧𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾॥௮॥  
𑌇𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌹𑌿𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌶𑍁𑌚𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌨𑌸𑌾 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑍌 𑌵𑌣𑌿𑌕𑍍॥௯॥  
𑌭𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌯𑌾 𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌕𑍁𑌟𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌬𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌯𑌾।  
𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌥𑍌 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌰𑍇 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍇 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௧௦॥  
𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍇𑌨 𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌨𑌾 𑌤𑌤𑌃।  
𑌜𑌗𑌾𑌮 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌸𑍌 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍁𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌰𑌨𑍍॥௧௧॥  
𑌤𑌤𑌃 𑌸 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍋 𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌶𑌾𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌧𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌿𑌰।  
𑌬𑌭𑍂𑌵 𑌚𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌮𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾॥௧௨॥  
𑌇𑌯𑌾𑌜 𑌸 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍈𑌃 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌰𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌣𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸 𑌦𑌦𑍌 𑌗𑍋𑌹𑌿𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌰𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌶𑌮𑍍॥௧௩॥  
𑌬𑍁𑌭𑍁𑌜𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌤𑍋 𑌭𑍋𑌗𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌰𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌨𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌨 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௧௪॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌭𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌾।  
𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍂𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌯𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿𑌃॥௧௫॥  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌏𑌕𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍁𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௧௬॥   
𑌉𑌦𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌕𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌸𑍈𑌃 𑌸𑌹।  
𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥௧௭॥   
𑌛𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌚 𑌗𑍋𑌭𑍂𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌨𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌤𑌮𑌂 𑌚𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌯𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌯𑌾॥௧௮॥   
𑌏𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌂 𑌕𑌿𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌤𑍁𑌮𑌿𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌸𑌿।  
𑌅𑌨𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌨 𑌮𑍇 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌨𑌘॥௧௯॥   
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍌 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍈𑌤𑌿 𑌹𑍁𑌤𑌂 𑌨 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂  
𑌤𑍇𑌨𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌿𑌭𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾।  
𑌉𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑍈𑌵𑌤𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌨𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌸𑍍-  
𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌿 𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌵॥௨௦॥  
  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌾𑌰𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌯𑍇---  
𑌅𑌥 𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 । 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾, 𑌸𑌾 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾  
𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌾, 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌹𑌿 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌧𑌰𑍀𑌯𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌗𑍋𑌭𑌿𑌲𑌃-  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑌃।  
𑌹𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌨 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌣𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾।  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇---  
𑌰𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮।  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌗𑌣𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌗𑌣𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾, 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌲𑌾𑌭𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌾।  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍋 𑌯𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌶𑌯𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥  
𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌶𑌯𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯-𑌯𑌵𑌦𑌾𑌨-𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌯-𑌫𑌲-𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿-𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌤𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌤𑍍 𑌫𑌲𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣𑍋𑌹𑌯𑌂 (𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍀𑌯𑌮𑍍)। 𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿  
𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌯𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍍। 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌯𑍇---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌤𑍋𑌯𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌿𑌲𑍍𑌬𑌿𑌷𑍈𑌃॥  
𑍐 𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌿𑌲𑍍𑌬𑌿𑌷𑌵𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌮𑍋 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌹𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇, 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌃।  
𑌕𑍌𑌶𑌿𑌕𑍀𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍇, 𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌯𑌣𑍇 𑌆𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇-  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌕𑌾𑌕𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌥 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑌾 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌃।  
𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌅𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌾 𑌋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌾 𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌕𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌖𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌕𑍌𑌶𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑍇 𑌵𑌸𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌰𑌃॥  
𑍐 𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌅𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌃 𑌕𑍌𑌶𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌹𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌃।  
𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌸𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍁𑌃---  
𑌇𑌯𑌮𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌿𑌕𑌾॥  
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌜𑍍𑌜𑌪𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌪𑌣𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌇𑌯𑌂 𑌰𑍋𑌹𑌿𑌣𑍀𑌬𑍁𑌧𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾॥  
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌣𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌯𑌃॥  
...  
𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍈𑌕𑌦𑍇𑌶𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿𑌨𑌾 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌯𑍇 𑌚𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌹𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍇 𑌪𑌰𑌾॥ 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍂𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍇 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾॥

4e7c5270bf.d: Budhaḥ rises out of combustion (udayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2026-Sep-11 19:54. At this moment budhaḥ is at uttaraphalgunī-4 kanyā (latitude 0°38′01.35″ N, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -0.66, elongation 12°41′13.56″ E of the Sun. Emergence from combustion restores a graha's full strength; this is generally considered an auspicious time to begin activities connected with budhaḥ's significations.

4ee0fa7a78.d: Guruḥ sets into combustion (astamayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2025-Jun-10 19:38. At this moment guruḥ is at mr̥gaśīrṣam-4 mithunam (latitude 0°09′45.30″ S, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -1.90, elongation 10°12′52.74″ E of the Sun. Combustion (mAudhyam) is generally considered to weaken a graha's ability to give full results in its significations; undertakings connected with guruḥ are traditionally best avoided until it re-emerges.

4f29c288c9.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°36′14.67″.
4f29c288c9.d:

4f55d6be48.d:
Beginning of Dhanurmasa puja in temples and at homes. A very early morning puja is performed, typically with mudgānnam as naivedyam. Begets fruit equivalent to performing puja for a thousand years!
The two ayana-s of the Sun are night and day for the Devas. 30 of these days become a month. The uṣahkāla of their day starts in chāpamāsa i.e. dhanurmāsa (although the shloka refers to the sidereal month, it appears logical to use the tropical month, owing to its association with uttarāyaṇam). Therefore, one must strive to perform uṣahkāla-pujā in this month, before sunrise --- a ṣōḍaśōpachāra-pūjā. Following this, one must perform Sandhyavandam and upasthanam! The Shivapurana also extols the uniqueness of the early morning puja in this month, suggesting that one must perform rudrābhiṣeka.

4f8e84dfcf.d:
The Abhidhyeyaka Abhishekam festival, also known as Jyeshthabhishekam, is a celebration held annually in the auspicious month of Jyeshtha, aligning with the Jyeshtha star in the constellation. The term “Abhidhyeyakam” refers to a protective shield or armour, symbolizing the divine defense that Bhagavan assumes in this Kaliyuga to combat evil. This festival, celebrated over three days, centers around a special abhishekam performed for this sacred armour.

According to temple traditions, this Abhishekam is conducted to safeguard the Utsava deities of Bhagavan Malayappa Swami and his consorts, Sridevi and Bhudevi. The purpose is to prevent any potential damage during various processions and holy baths (Tirumanjanam) throughout the year.

Each day of the festival, after the second bell, the deities are taken to the Kalyanotsava Mandapam situated in Sampangi Prakaram. Here, Snapana Tirumanjanam is performed, a ritual involving bathing the deities with consecrated water infused with spices, turmeric, sandal paste, honey, milk, and curd, accompanied by the chanting of Vedic mantras.

On each day, Bhagavan and his consorts are adorned in unique kavachams: The first day features the Vajrakavacham, a diamond-studded armour; the second day showcases the Muthyala kavacham, an armour studded with pearls; and the third day highlights the Svarna kavacham, a golden armour. The Svarna kavacham remains on the deities for the entire year and is only removed for the next Abhidhyeyaka Abhishekam.

4fcbd26044.b: Observed on Svātī nakshatra of Dhanuḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
4fcbd26044.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

In the fertile region of Kancharur within the Chola kingdom, a devout follower of Bhagavan Shiva named Manakancharanar, the 12th Nayanmar, lived. Belonging to a Vellala family and respected as a hereditary Senathipathi, he was known for his ability to intuitively serve Shiva Bhaktas without them having to ask. After a long period without children, his devout prayers were answered with the birth of a daughter, whose arrival he celebrated with extensive charity.

As the daughter grew and reached marriageable age, she was betrothed to Eyarkon Kalikamar, another sincere devotee of Bhagavan Shiva. The wedding was planned, but before it could take place, Bhagavan Shiva decided to bestow a special blessing upon Manakancharanar. Assuming the guise of a Maha-Vrathiar, a holy man with distinctive ash markings and a garland of bones, Bhagavan Shiva appeared before Manakancharanar. Inquiring about the festive preparations, the ascetic learned of the impending wedding and expressed a desire for the bride's hair to make a Panchavati, a sacred thread.

Without hesitation and disregarding the potential consequences, including the possibility of the groom rejecting his disfigured daughter, Manakancharanar cut off his daughter's hair and offered it to the ascetic. Immediately after, Bhagavan Shiva revealed his true form to Manakancharanar and his family, blessing them.

When Eyarkon Kalikamar and his party arrived and learned of the incident, they were disappointed on missing out on the darshan of Bhagavan Shiva. Further, they were dismayed to see the disfigured bride, but Bhagavan Shiva, understanding the situation, restored the daughter's hair! Relieved and overjoyed, Manakancharanar and his family proceeded with the wedding.

These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

The 4th of the Nayanmars was Ilayankudi Mara Nayanmar, a farmer named Maranar from the village of Ilayankudi. He was a devout follower of Bhagavan Shiva and His devotees. He practiced Maaheswara Puja, a form of worship involving honouring and serving Bhagavan Shiva's devotees with utmost reverence, as if serving Bhagavan Himself. This included welcoming devotees, washing their feet, offering them food, and treating them with great respect and kindness.

Though Nayanmar was blessed with wealth, he believed his riches were meant to serve Bhagavan's devotees. His devotion remained steadfast even as his wealth dwindled. Eventually, he sold all his possessions and even himself to continue serving the devotees.

One rainy day, with no food at home, Nayanmar and his wife were visited by a Shiva Bhakta. Despite their own hunger, they welcomed the devotee warmly. Nayanmar's wife suggested gathering the grain-seeds they had recently sown to prepare a meal. After they fed the devotee and Nayanmar went to check on him, he found the devotee had vanished. Instead, Bhagavan Shiva and Mother Parvathy appeared in the sky, revealing that the devotee was Bhagavan Shiva in disguise. They blessed Nayanmar and his wife for their unwavering devotion and promised them eternal life in the divine abode. This story exemplifies the profound impact of selfless service and devotion to the Supreme and His devotees.
